questions.question_text: Tay-Sachs disease is caused by deficiency of
questions.explanation:
Tay-Sachs disease belongs to the group of autosomal-recessive lysosomal storage metabolic disorders. It is caused by hexosaminidase A (Hex A) enzyme deficiency. In most cases, the disease manifests itself during infancy, which characterises the most severe disorders of the nervous system. The typical features are muscle weakness, ataxia, speech, and mental disorders. Currently disease treatment is based on symptom relief.
Ref: Solovyeva VV et al. New approaches to Tay-Sachs disease therapy. Frontiers in physiology. 2018:1663.

questions.question_text: The anticipation in paternal transmission is most likely to show up in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Huntington disease is characterised by the phenomenon of anticipation, where the age of onset tends to decrease in successive generations. This decrease is due to the unstable nature of the CAG repeats that tend to increase in size, particularly when passed through the male germline. Although germline instability can explain the phenomenon of anticipation, somatic instability has been proposed as a mechanism underlying the tissue specificity of the disease.
Ref: Jimenez-Sanchez M et al. Huntington’s disease: mechanisms of pathogenesis and therapeutic strategies. Cold Spring Harbor perspectives in medicine. 2017 Jul 1;7(7):a024240.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is most likely with regard to Fragile X syndrome?

options.text: Clinical features are apparent only during adolescence
Intelligence is correlated to the load of chromosomal damage

correct_answer.text: Intelligence is correlated to the load of chromosomal damage

correct_answers.text: Intelligence is correlated to the load of chromosomal damage

questions.explanation:
Fragile X syndrome (FXS) is the most common single gene disorder, which causes autism and intellectual disability. The fragile X mental retardation 1 (FMR1) gene is silenced when CGG Triplet repeats exceed 200, which is the full mutation that causes FXS. Carriers of FXS have a CGG repeat of between 55 and 200, which is defined as a premutation and transcription of the gene is overactive with high levels of the FMR1 mRNA. Most carriers of the premutation have normal levels of fragile X mental retardation protein (FMRP) and a normal intelligence, but in the upper range of the premutation (120-200) the FMRP level may be lower than normal. The clinical problems associated with the premutation are caused by the RNA toxicity associated with increased FMR1mRNA levels, although for some mildly lowered FMRP can cause problems associated with FXS.
Ref: Tassanakijpanich N et al. Fragile X premutation and associated health conditions: A review. Clinical Genetics. 2021 Jun;99(6):751-60.

questions.explanation:
The anterior insula is crucial in transforming unpleasant sensory input into visceromotor reactions and the accompanying feeling of disgust.
Cantone M et al. Fear and disgust: case report of two uncommon emotional disturbances evoked by visual disperceptions after a right temporal-insular stroke. BMC neurology. 2019 Dec;19(1):1-4.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is seen in anterior cerebral artery occlusion?
questions.explanation: Occlusion of the anterior cerebral artery may result in weakness and sensory loss of the contralateral foot and leg; gait apraxia and urinary incontinence (with bilateral damage in the acute phase). This sometimes resembles the triad of Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus where identical anatomical structures are implicated albeit presenting with an insidious or subacute onset. In left-sided lesions, some cases present with transcortical motor aphasia.

questions.question_text: A 56-year-old gentleman suffers from ataxia and nystagmus. His CT scan shows ischemia in cerebellum. Which part of cerebellum is most likely to be affected?
questions.explanation:
The flocculonodular lobe is the evolutionarily oldest part of the cerebellum, consisting of a pair of irregular structures (flocculi) joined in the middle by a node or nodulus and separated by a deep fissure from the back of the cerebellum, connected to the vestibular system and concerned chiefly with posture, balance, and ballistic movements.
Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: Which area of the brain is implicated with recognition of faces?
questions.explanation:
The fusiform gyrus is a spindle-shaped gyrus on the medial (inside) surface of each temporal lobe, at the junction of the occipital lobe, occupied by Area V4 of the visual cortex, largely responsible for colour perception and also implicated in face recognition. Face perception is an ability that involves many areas of the brain. Brain imaging studies have typically shown a great deal of activity in the fusiform gyrus, an area also known to cause prosopagnosia when damaged bilaterally.
Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: Which of the following enzymes is responsible for the degradation of noradrenaline?
questions.explanation:
Norepinephrine (NE) action is terminated by two principal destructive or catabolic enzymes that turn NE into inactive metabolites. The first is monoamine oxidase A or B, which is located in mitochondria in the presynaptic neuron and elsewhere. The second is catechol-O- methyltransferase (COMT), which is thought to be located largely outside of the presynaptic nerve terminal. The action of NE can be terminated not only by enzymes that destroy NE, but also by a transport pump for NE that removes it from acting in the synapse without destroying it.
Ref: Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Neuroscientific Basis and Practical Applications, 5th Edition. 2021. pp. 253-254.

questions.question_text: Which of the following substance is the most active ingredient in the Ethiopian plant Catha edulis, whose leaves on chewing provide amphetamine-like stimulation?
questions.explanation:
Catha edulis, or ‘Khat’, is a plant indigenous to Eastern Africa and Southern Arabia. It releases a variety of psychoactive chemicals, including the stimulants cathinone and cathine. Khat is chewed like tobacco and held between the cheek and gums after chewing. The stimulant effect of the Khat plant was originally attributed to cathine, but this was disputed by reports showing the plant extracts from fresh leaves contained another substance more active than cathine - called cathinone. Cathinone is not very stable and breaks down to produce cathine and norephedrine. This explains why fresh leaves are more stimulating, and the habit of chewing Khat is more or less confined to the regions where it is cultivated.
In the mid-2000s, synthetic cathinones began to appear, marketed as ‘legal high’ chemicals. They were packaged under labels including ‘screen cleaner’, ‘jewelry cleaner’, and most notoriously ‘bath salts’. These compounds are substituted cathinones that are chemically modified to avoid regulatory control. Generally, substituted cathinones increase synaptic catecholamine levels by inhibiting the dopamine, serotonin, and norepinephrine reuptake transporters in a fashion similar to cocaine. Most also facilitate catecholamine release, similar to methamphetamine.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 303.

questions.question_text: Hyperpolarization of the neuron is influenced by which of the following?
questions.explanation: In CNS neurons, inhibitory transmitters open chloride channels. In addition, second messengers that mediate inhibition work by operating on potassium channels.

questions.question_text: The receptors which have both pre and postsynaptic presence are
questions.explanation:
Dopamine receptors are divided into two groups. The first group is the D1-like receptors, including both D1 and D5 receptors. D1-like receptors are excitatory, and positively linked to adenylate cyclase. The second group is the D2-like receptors, including D2, D3, and D4 receptors. D2-like receptors are inhibitory and negatively linked to adenylate cyclase. Thus, the neurotransmitter DA can be either excitatory or inhibitory, depending on which DA receptor it binds. All five DA receptors can be located postsynaptically, but D2 and D3 receptors can also both be located presynaptically, where, due to their inhibitory actions, they act as autoreceptors to inhibit further DA release.
Ref: Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Neuroscientific Basis and Practical Applications, 5th Edition. 2021. pp. 81-82.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the most powerful endogenous opioid peptide?
questions.explanation:
Dynorphin A has been described as ‘extraordinarily potent’ (‘dyn from the Greek, dynamis = power and ‘orphin’ for the endogenous morphine peptide). Dynorphin peptides are released in the brain during stress exposure. After they are released, they activate kappa opioid receptors distributed throughout the brain and spinal cord, where they trigger cellular responses resulting in different stress responses: analgesia, dysphoria-like behaviours, anxiety-like responses, and increased addiction behaviours in experimental animals.
Ref: Chavkin C. Dynorphin–still an extraordinarily potent opioid peptide. Molecular pharmacology. 2013 Apr 1;83(4):729-36.

questions.question_text: All of the following intrauterine infections cause intellectual disabilities except
questions.explanation:
Maternal infections during pregnancy, especially viral infections, have been known to cause fetal damage and intellectual disability. Syphilis (caused by Treponema pallidum) in pregnant women was once the leading cause of various neuropathic changes in their offspring, including intellectual disability. Rubella (German measles) has now replaced syphilis as the primary cause of congenital malformations and intellectual disability caused by maternal infection. Children with intellectual disability from cytomegalovirus frequently have cerebral calcification, microcephaly, or hydrocephalus. Toxoplasmosis causes mild to severe intellectual disability and, in severe cases, hydrocephalus, seizures, microcephaly, and chorioretinitis. EBV (Infectious Mononucleosis) has not been implicated in intellectual disability syndromes.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 104.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is least likely to occur in schizophrenia?
questions.explanation:
Macroscopic brain changes that occur in schizophrenia include enlarged ventricle size and reductions in grey matter volume, whole-brain volume, and white matter anisotropy. The reduced neuropil (intertwined axons and dendrites of neurons) hypothesis has been suggested as a microanatomical explanation to account for these macroscopic changes. Studies have found both increased and decreased neuronal density in the cerebral cortex. The literature provides support for increased neuron density in schizophrenia, with variation dependent on age. Although the brain is abnormal, gliosis is absent.
Ref: Bakhshi K, Chance SA. The neuropathology of schizophrenia: a selective review of past studies and emerging themes in brain structure and cytoarchitecture. Neuroscience. 2015 Sep 10;303:82-102.
Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 189.

questions.question_text: An intravenous heroin user presents with significant slowing of cognitive ability. He has fatuous affect and impaired concentration that has developed insidiously. Which of the following is a likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder (HAND) is an umbrella term for the spectrum of neurocognitive impairment induced by HIV (direct effects of HIV). It ranges from asymptomatic impairment to severe impairment with pronounced deficits in self-efficacy and interference with day-to-day activities. Early indicators of HAND include impairments in psychomotor function, in simple and divided attention and concentration, in mental agility, and in mental flexibility. HAND also relates to personality changes (e.g. apathy, irritability, and inertia) and changes in behaviour (e.g. social withdrawal and impaired activities of daily living). Neurological signs of HAND include poor concentration, loss of balance, and tremor.
Ref: Knights MJ et al. HIV infection and its psychiatric manifestations: a clinical overview. BJPsych Advances. 2017 Jul;23(4):265-77
Taylor DM, Gaughran F, Pillinger T. The Maudsley Practice Guidelines for Physical Health Conditions in Psychiatry. 2021.

Explanation: Beta waves have a frequency of more than 13 Hz.
Ref: Boutros NN, Galderisi S, Pogarell O, Riggio S. Standard electroencephalography in clinical psychiatry: A practical handbook. 2011.

questions.question_text: The disorder associated with ambiguous genitalia is
questions.explanation:
The congenital adrenal hyperplasias comprise a family of autosomal recessive disorders that disrupt adrenal steroidogenesis. Infant females with classical congenital adrenal hyperplasia generally present in the neonatal period with ambiguous genitalia.
Ref: Witchel SF. Congenital adrenal hyperplasia. Journal of pediatric and adolescent gynecology. 2017 Oct 1;30(5):520-34.

questions.question_text: A 58 year old man presents with postural hypotension, anorexia, nausea and weakness. He appears to be extremely apathetic, with significant anhedonia compounded by fatigue and depressed mood.Which of the following hormonal imbalance is most likely?
questions.explanation:
Addison syndrome may result from adrenal destruction by autoimmune disease, metastatic cancer, tuberculosis, or human immunodeficiency virus infection or secondary to suppression of ACTH secretion by chronic corticosteroid therapy. Addison disease (primary adrenal insufficiency) is characterised by chronic glucocorticoid and/or mineralocorticoid deficiency due to failure of the adrenal cortex. It should be suspected in all acutely or chronically ill patients with general fatigue or severe weakness and unexplained dehydration, hypotension, weight loss, fever, abdominal pain, and hyperpigmentation. Psychiatric symptoms include apathy, anhedonia, fatigue, and depressed mood. It may be misdiagnosed as major depressive disorder. Anorexia is common in both depression and Addison disease, but the presence of nausea, vomiting and hyperpigmentation may suggest Addison disease.
Ref: Barthel A et al. An update on Addison’s disease. Experimental and Clinical Endocrinology & Diabetes. 2019 Feb;127(02/03):165-75.

questions.question_text: Choose the antidepressant which, if given to a pregnant mother, is most likely to cause withdrawal symptoms in the neonate?
questions.explanation:
When antidepressants are taken during pregnancy, the neonate may experience discontinuation symptoms, which are usually mild, such as agitation and irritability, or rarely respiratory distress and convulsions (with SSRIs). The risk is assumed to be particularly high with short half- life drugs such as paroxetine and venlafaxine. Continuing to breastfeed and then ‘weaning’ by switching to mixed (breast/bottle) feeding may help reduce the severity of reactions.
Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 689.

questions.question_text: The drug that is most likely to result in a hypertensive crisis from the given list is
questions.explanation:
The most worrisome side effect of MAOIs (such as phenelzine) is the tyramine-induced hypertensive crisis (‘cheese reaction’). The amino acid tyramine is normally transformed via GI metabolism. However, MAOIs inactivate GI metabolism of dietary tyramine, thus allowing intact tyramine to enter the circulation. A hypertensive crisis may subsequently occur because of a powerful pressor effect of the amino acid.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 645.

questions.question_text: Lucy on antidepressant medication for more than 8 years. She has developed pins and needles and a burning type of pain on her feet and legs. The most likely offending medication is
questions.explanation:
Among the most common drugs that can cause toxic neuropathies are phenelzine and phenytoin. Phenelzine has a higher likelihood of causing peripheral neuropathy than the other antidepressants listed here.
Ref: Grisold W, Carozzi VA. Toxicity in Peripheral Nerves: An Overview. Toxics. 2021 Sep;9(9):218.

questions.question_text: A 50-year-old lady on treatment with Tranylcypromine consumed cheese and developed hypertensive reaction. What is the most suitable choice for treatment of this condition?
questions.explanation:
An MAOI-induced hypertensive crisis should be treated with alpha-adrenergic antagonists (for example phentolamine or chlorpromazine). These drugs lower blood pressure within 5 minutes. IV furosemide can be used to reduce fluid load, and a beta-adrenergic receptor antagonist can control tachycardia.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 646.

questions.explanation: Pregnancy is an obvious cause of amenorrhea and is the most common reason for secondary amenorrhea.

questions.question_text: The best treatment among the following for lithium induced tremors is
questions.explanation:
Early adverse effects of lithium include gastrointestinal upset and fine tremor. Propranolol can be useful in lithium-induced tremor. Course tremor is associated with lithium toxicity and may be seen together with muscle weakness/twitching, drowsiness, confusion, and ataxia.
Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 250.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a significant risk factor for the development of antidepressant induced SIADH?
questions.explanation:
Most antidepressants have been associated with hyponatraemia. It has been suggested that serotonergic drugs are relatively more likely than noradrenergic drugs to cause hypnonatraemia, although this is disputed. Risk factors include: older age (most important), female sex, major surgery, history of hyponatraemia or a low baseline sodium concentration, co-therapy with other drugs known to be associated hyponatraemia (e.g. diuretics, NSAIDs, antipsychotics, carbamazepine, cancer chemotherapy, calcium antagonists, ACE inhibitors, and laxatives), reduced renal function, medical co-morbidity (e.g. hypothyroidism, diabetes, COPD, hypertension, head injury, congestive cardiac failure, cerebrovascular accident, various cancers), and low body weight.
Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. pp. 393-394.

questions.question_text: Which of the following has been associated with the use of SSRIs in mid-late pregnancy?
questions.explanation:
A specific problem that has been associated with serotonergic antidepressant use in mid to late pregnancy is persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN). Although initial reports suggested an approximate six-fold increase, recent literature has shown the absolute risk to be small and more modest. Although the risk of PPHN in babies exposed in utero to SSRIs is increased, the absolute risk is low.
Ref: McAllister-Williams RH et al. British Association for Psychopharmacology consensus guidance on the use of psychotropic medication preconception, in pregnancy and postpartum 2017. Journal of Psychopharmacology. 2017 May;31(5):519-52.

questions.question_text: What effect can carbamazepine have on cardiac function?
questions.explanation:
Carbamazepine decreases cardiac conduction and can thus exacerbate pre-existing cardiac disease. Carbamazepine use rarely elicits an immune hypersensitivity response consisting of fever, rash, eosinophilia, and possibly fatal myocarditis. Carbamazepine can cause sinus tachycardia.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 661.
Taylor DM, Gaughran F, Pillinger T. The Maudsley Practice Guidelines for Physical Health Conditions in Psychiatry. 2021. p. 5.

questions.question_text: Deaths in neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) are usually due to
questions.explanation:
Deaths from neuroleptic malignant syndrome are usually due to respiratory failure, cardiovascular collapse, myoglobinuric renal failure, sepsis, arrythmias, thromboembolism, or disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC).
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 1018.

questions.question_text: Which one among the following is more likely to induce akathisia?
questions.explanation:
The relative liability of individual antipsychotic medications for akathisia is uncertain, but there is consensus that the incidence is lowest for olanzapine, quetiapine, and clozapine. The incidence of akathisia is relatively high with haloperidol, risperidone, aripiprazole, and ziprasidone.
Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. pp. 110, 114.

questions.question_text: Mr.X is a 33 year old gentleman with a long standing diagnosis of paranoid schizophrenia. He was started on atypical anti psychotic medication 6 months ago and when reviewed in the clinic, he complains of side effects such as reduced sexual function and has also developed enlarged breasts. Which of the following anti psychotic drugs is most likely to be associated with these side effects?
questions.explanation:
When D2 antagonists are administered, D2 receptors in the tuberoinfundibular dopamine pathway are blocked. This causes plasma prolactin concentrations to rise, a condition called hyperprolactinaemia. This can be associated with galactorrhea (i.e. breast secretions), sexual dysfunction, gynaecomastia (enlargement of the breasts) in men, and amenorrhea (i.e. irregular or lack of menstrual periods) in women.
Ref: Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Neuroscientific Basis and Practical Applications, 5th Edition. 2021. pp. 164-165.
Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 168.

questions.question_text: The site of action of thyroid hormones is at the level of;
questions.explanation: Thyroid hormones diffuse through cell membranes to bind with receptors that are members of a large super-family of nuclear receptors that act as hormonally-activated transcription factors. The hormone-receptor complex interacts with the DNA of to activate gene transcription processes downstream.

questions.question_text: Zolpidem acts as an agonist at
questions.explanation:
Z drugs bind to benzodiazepine-sensitive GABA-A receptors. A different nomenclature (omega system) denotes the specific sites of GABA-A receptors where these ‘Z’ drugs act as omega-1 receptors. Conventional benzodiazepines interact at both ω1 and ω2 sites, the latter likely contributing to side effects.
Zolpidem and zaleplon bind selectively to alpha-1 subunits of these sites. By contrast, benzodiazepines, zopiclone and eszopiclone bind to four alpha subunits (alpha-1, alpha-2, alpha-3, and alpha-5). The functional significance of alpha-1 selectivity is not yet proven, but may contribute to lower risk of tolerance and dependence. The alpha-1 subtype is known to be critical for producing sedation and thus is targeted by every effective GABA-A PAM (positive allosteric modulator) hypnotic, both benzodiazepines and Z-drugs.
Ref: Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Neuroscientific Basis and Practical Applications, 5th Edition. 2021. pp. 422-423.
Madari S, Golebiowski R, Mansukhani MP, Kolla BP. Pharmacological management of insomnia. Neurotherapeutics. 2021 Jan;18(1):44-52.

questions.question_text: Which of the following medications is not associated with an increased risk of depression?
questions.explanation:
Orlistat interferes with the absorption of dietary fats, causing reduced caloric intake. It works by inhibiting gastric and pancreatic lipases, the enzymes that break down triglycerides in the intestine. The most common subjective side effects of orlistat are GI related and include steatorrhea, flatulence, fecal incontinence, and frequent or urgent bowel movements. Hepatic and renal injuries are potentially severe side effects or orlistat use. It has not been associated with an increased risk of depression.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. pp. 708-709.

questions.question_text: Which of the following selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors has notable anticholinergic activity?
questions.explanation:
Paroxetine has the highest anticholinergic effects of the SSRIs. Paroxetine’s mild anticholinergic actions can enhance the rapid onset of anxiolytic and hypnotic efficacy, but also cause mild anticholinergic side effects.
Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. pp. 421-422.
Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Prescriber’s Guide, 7th Edition. 2021. p. 599.

questions.question_text: Risperidone increases the levels of
questions.explanation:
When D2 antagonists, such as risperidone, are administered, D2 receptors in the tuberoinfundibular dopamine pathway are blocked. This causes plasma prolactin concentrations to rise, a condition called hyperprolactinaemia. This can be associated with galactorrhea (i.e. breast secretions), sexual dysfunction, gynaecomastia (enlargement of the breasts) in men, and amenorrhea (i.e. irregular or lack of menstrual periods) in women.
Ref: Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Neuroscientific Basis and Practical Applications, 5th Edition. 2021. pp. 164-165.

questions.question_text: Which combination could be prescribed together, in which the second drug is used to minimize the adverse effect of the first one?
questions.explanation:
Reboxetine is a selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor. Side effects may appear ‘anticholinergic’, but reboxetine does not directly block muscarinic receptors. Constipation, dry mouth, and urinary retention are noradrenergic, due in part to peripheral alpha 1 receptor stimulation causing decreased acetylcholine release. Thus, antidotes for these side effects can be alpha 1 antagonists such as tamsulosin or doxazosin, especially in men over 50 with borderline urine flow.
Ref: Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Prescriber’s Guide, 7th Edition. 2021. p. 684.

questions.question_text: What happens to GABA-A receptors in benzodiazepine withdrawal state?

options.text: Reduced inhibitory tone in the CNS

questions.explanation: Chronic benzodiazepine administration may lead to uncoupling of the linkage between GABAA and benzodiazepine receptor sites and subsequent preferential degradation of certain GABAA receptor units. Such a change results in a long-term homeostatic adaptation to the chronic presence of benzodiazepines leading to a reduction in GABA receptor density. Sudden withdrawal of the benzodiazepine once tolerance has developed would expose the recipient to underactive GABA system without the counterbalancing presence of benzodiazepine drugs.

questions.question_text: A middle-aged gentleman suffers from alcohol withdrawal symptoms and has history of liver impairment. A suitable drug for detoxification would be;
questions.explanation:
Shorter-acting benzodiazepines (e.g. oxazepam) may be preferred in those for whom over-sedation must be avoided, in people with liver disease who may not be able to metabolise long-acting agents efficiently, and in people with COPD. However, there is a greater risk of breakthrough seizures and greater potential for misuse.
Ref: National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence. The NICE guideline on diagnosis, assessment and management of harmful drinking and alcohol dependence. Updated edition 2020.

questions.question_text: Which one among the following is more related to causing discontinuation syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Discontinuation effects can be more common or more severe with paroxetine than with other SSRIs. Paroxetine’s discontinuation effects may be related to the fact that it inhibits its own metabolism. Thus, when paroxetine is withdrawn, the rate of its decline can be faster as it stops inhibiting its metabolism. Readaptation of cholinergic receptors after prolonged blockade may also contribute to the discontinuation effects of paroxetine.
Ref: Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Prescriber’s Guide, 7th Edition. 2021. p. 596.

questions.question_text: Which of the following drugs follows zero-order kinetics?
questions.explanation:
Phenytoin follows zero-order kinetics.
Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 836.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is correct with regard to the pharmacokinetics of depot antipsychotics?

options.text: Test doses are not useful to avoid severe adverse effects
Higher doses are significantly more effective than lower doses
Adverse effects are usually short lived than oral medications due to the low frequency of administration
Plasma level of depot antipsychotics could be as high as 4 times the initial levels, 2 to 3 months after starting treatment
Shortening the dosing intervals can improve efficacy in non-responders

correct_answer.text: Plasma level of depot antipsychotics could be as high as 4 times the initial levels, 2 to 3 months after starting treatment

correct_answers.text: Plasma level of depot antipsychotics could be as high as 4 times the initial levels, 2 to 3 months after starting treatment

questions.explanation:
For first-generation antipsychotic (FGA) depots, a test dose should be given. Because of its long half-life, any adverse effects from the administration of a depot are likely to be long-lived. For FGAs, a test dose consisting of a small dose of active drug in a small volume of oil serves a dual purpose: it is a test of the patient’s sensitivity to EPS and of any sensitivity to the base oil. For second-generation antipsychotic (SGA) depots, test doses may not be required (less propensity to cause EPS and aqueous base not known to be allergenic) although they could be considered appropriate where a patient is suspected of being non-adherent to oral antipsychotic medication and the depot will be the first exposure to guaranteed antipsychotic medication delivery. For both types of depots, prior treatment with the equivalent oral formulation is preferred to assess efficacy and tolerability. At the start of therapy, plasma drug levels increase over several weeks to months without increasing the given dose. (This is due to accumulation: steady state is only achieved after at least 6-8 weeks.) There are few data showing clear dose-response effects for depots. There is some information indicating that low doses (within the licensed range) may be at least as effective as higher ones. Depots should be administered at the longest possible licensed interval. There is no evidence to suggest that shortening the dose interval improves efficacy.
Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. pp. 67-68.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the most important property of a depot antipsychotic medication?

options.text: The elimination is almost entirely renal

questions.explanation: Depot antipsychotics are esters formed between the alcohol group of the antipsychotic compound and a long chain of fatty acids (enantic, decanoic, palmitic, and undecylenic acid), and this ester is dissolved in oil (sesame oil or Viscoleo). Antipsychotic compounds are generally fat-soluble, but the esterification increases this fat solubility 1000 times (the longer the carbon chain of the fatty acid esters, the more the fat solubility). The ester is released from the oil phase by slow diffusion into the body water phase. The higher the fat solubility, the slower the release. (Kane et al., European Neuropsychopharmacology 1998, 8: 55-56)

questions.question_text: Mrs. P suffers from bipolar disorder and is on lithium carbonate treatment. She also suffers from systemic hypertension. The ideal drug of choice for treating her hypertension would be
questions.explanation:
ACE inhibitors (e.g. captopril, ramipril) can reduce thirst (which can lead to mild dehydration) and increase renal sodium loss (leading to increased sodium re-absorption by the kidney), resulting in an increase in lithium plasma levels. The magnitude of this effect is variable, from no increase to a four-fold increase. Care is also required with angiotensin II receptor antagonists such as candesartan. Diuretics can reduce the renal clearance of lithium, the magnitude of this effect being greater with thiazide than loop diuretics. Lithium levels usually rise within 10 days of a thiazide diuretic (e.g. bendroflumethiazide, chlortalidone, inadapamide, xipamide) being prescribed. Beta-blockers like propranalol are relatively safe to be used with lithium.
Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. pp. 252-253.

questions.question_text: Pharmacokinetic properties of SSRIs include all except

options.text: Presence of active metabolite with longer half life for certain compounds
Requirement for a washout period prior to administration of an MAOI
Non linear elimination kinetics in high doses

questions.explanation:
SSRIs are well, but not rapidly, absorbed after oral administration. They have their peak effects in the range of 3-8 hours. Absorption of sertraline may be slightly enhanced by food. All SSRIs have a long half-life, which allows once daily administration. Fluoxetine has the most prolonged half-life: 4-6 days; its active metabolite has a half-life of 7-9 days. The half-life of sertraline is 26 hours, and its less active metabolite has a half-life of 3-5 days. Fluoxetine displays non-linear kinetics probably owing to the saturation of liver enzymes. Higher doses can result in disproportionately higher plasma levels.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 625.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct option regarding effects of smoking?
questions.explanation:
Tobacco smoke contains polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons that induce (increase the activity of) certain hepatic enzymes (CYP1A2 in particular). The extent of enzyme induction is determined by the number and type of cigarettes smoked and the degree of smoke inhalation. For some drugs used in psychiatry, smoking significantly reduces drug plasma levels and higher doses are required than in non-smokers. Smoking reduces plasma clozapine levels by up to 50%.
Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 856.

questions.question_text: A child attains gender identity in which stage of Freud's psychosexual development?
questions.explanation:
The phallic stage begins sometime during year 3 and continues until approximately the end of year 5. The phallic stage lays the foundation for gender identity and serves to integrate residues from the previous stages into a predominantly genital-sexual orientation.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1062-1063.

questions.question_text: At your CAMHS inpatient unit, you observe Paolo, a four-year-old boy playing with his dinosaur toy. He treats it as though it is a living object. According to Piaget's model, which stage of cognitive development is he in?
questions.explanation:
Explanation.
This child is displaying animism. In Piaget’s pre-operational stage, children use animistic thinking, which is the tendency to endow physical events and objects with life-like psychological attributes, such as feelings and intentions.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1008.

questions.question_text: Pauline is a first-time mother to Stephanie, her 18-month-old daughter. She is worried that Stephanie isn't talking as well as the other children at the nursery. If an 18-month-old child has normal development, how many words should he or she know at this stage?
questions.explanation:
By age 18 months, a child is generally using 20 single words. They will understand up to 150 words.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 889.

questions.question_text: In your CAMHS clinic, you observe Mollie, a five-year-old girl, as she plays with her doll. You notice that she is talking to her doll as though it is real. What is the name of this phenomenon?
questions.explanation:
Animism is the belief that plants, inanimate objects and natural phenomena possess a living soul and have human-like feelings and intentions. In Piaget’s pre-operational stage, children use such animistic thinking to endow physical events and objects with life-like psychological attributes, such as feelings and intentions.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1008.

questions.question_text: According to Kohlberg, which one among the following represent Conventional Stage?
questions.explanation:
Lawrence Kohlberg integrated Jean Piaget’s concepts and described multiple stages of moral development within three significant levels of morality. The first level is pre-conventional morality, in which punishment and obedience are the determining factors. The second level is morality of conventional role-conformity, in which children try to conform to gain approval and maintain good relationships with others and are also guided by rigid codes of ‘law and order’ (authority orientation). The third and highest level is the morality of self-accepted moral principles (post-conventional), in which children voluntarily comply with rules based on a concept of universal ethical principles and make exceptions to rules in certain circumstances.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 902.
Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is seen in a normal child development?

options.text: Babbling with consonant sounds at 7 months
Putting two words together at 4 years

correct_answer.text: Babbling with consonant sounds at 7 months

correct_answers.text: Babbling with consonant sounds at 7 months

questions.explanation: Babbling is the production of articulate sounds that are not yet recognizable words. It begins shortly after birth. At around 7 months, babbling contains alternations of vowels and consonants e.g. baba, mama (Ref. NHS)

questions.question_text: In a strange situation experiment, Bobby, a 2-year-old boy, is only comforted when his mother returns to the room and is not comforted by the stranger. What type of attachment is seen here?
questions.explanation:
Mary Ainsworth devised the Strange Situation procedure with 12- to 18-month infants, which categorised infant-parent relationships. The procedure involves separations and reunions with caregivers and observes response. In secure attachment, the child is distressed by separation but can quickly be soothed on reunion with the caregiver.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. pp. 658-659.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT a risk factor for delayed speech development?
questions.explanation: The important family risk factors associated with delayed language development in children include large family size, smoking in pregnancy, rapid successive pregnancies, absence of father, low levels of parental education, divorce, marital disharmony & violence.

questions.question_text: Which of the following has the strongest correlation with developmental language delay?
questions.explanation: Smoking during pregnancy and large family size are the strongest risk factors for developmental language delay

questions.question_text: The preferential attachment of a baby to one adult female figure is called;
questions.explanation:
Attachment theory originated in the work of John Bowlby. Being monotropic, infants tend to attach to one person, but they can form attachments to several people. A basic sense of security and safety is derived from a continuous and close relationship with a caregiver, usually the mother.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1011.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is an objective test of personality?
questions.explanation:
The Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory (MMPI) is a self-report questionnaire consisting of 567 questions covering eight areas of psychopathology and two areas of personality type. The scales are: Hypochondriasis, Depression, Hysteria, Psychopathic deviate, Masculinity-femininity, Paranoia, Psychasthenia, Schizophrenia, Hypomania, and Social introversion. There are also four additional validity (test-taking attitude) scales. It is NOT a projective test.
Projective tests of personality include the Rorschach test, Thematic Apperception Test (TAT), Sentence Completion Test, Holtzman Inkblot Technique (TIT), Figure drawing (typically human forms but can involve houses or other forms) and Make-a-Picture Story (MAPS). Projective tests use ambiguous stimuli, and the patient is expected to generate narratives based on them; rating scales may or may not be used in conjunction to rate such measures.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 96.
Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.
Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 59.

questions.question_text: The best neuropsychological test of semantic memory is

options.text: Naming objects and describing their meanings

correct_answer.text: Naming objects and describing their meanings

correct_answers.text: Naming objects and describing their meanings

questions.explanation:
Semantic memory is a type of long-term memory for factual information about the world, excluding personal episodes in one’s life. Typical examples are knowledge of the dates of the world wars and the chemical formula for water. The term is from the Greek ‘semantikos’, so called because it is necessary for the use of language.
Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: Which of the following scales utilizes the theory of Big Five personality constructs?
questions.explanation:
NEO stands for Neuroticism, Extraversion, and Openness to experience. The inventory is a questionnaire designed to measure the Big Five personality factors, namely those three plus Agreeableness and Conscientiousness.
Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: In Skinner box experiments, rats receive food pellets in response to pressing a lever. What type of learning is this?
questions.explanation:
The basic principles of operant conditioning are that if a response to a stimulus produces positive consequences for the individual, it will tend to be repeated, while if it is followed by negative consequences, it will not. In Thorndike and Skinner’s original experiments, rats were placed in a box containing a level that, when pressed, delivered a pellet of food. Eventually, the rat would press the lever and be rewarded. The rat would then press the lever with increasing frequency.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 907.

questions.question_text: Star charts are effective in managing certain behavioural problems. They work on the basis of
questions.explanation:
Behaviour modification is based on operant conditioning. Forms of behavioural modification include the use of secondary reinforcement, such as ‘token economy’, in which socially desirable/acceptable behaviours are rewarded with tokens that can be exchanged for other material items or privileges, or ‘star charts’ where children’s good behaviour is rewarded when a certain level is achieved.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 908.

questions.question_text: A child was told to finish homework tasks before he can play outside. This is based on
questions.explanation:
The Premack principle asserts that access to a preferred action will reinforce any action that is less preferred. Any behaviour that is preferred to a second behaviour will theoretically reinforce the second behaviour.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1019.

questions.question_text: With respect to memorising a list of words, which one among the following statements is true?

options.text: In immediate recall the primacy effect is stronger than the recency effect
The retroactive inhibition refers to prior learning interfering with subsequent learning
Primacy effect is related to initial items receiving most consolidation
Elaborative rehearsal helps to store information in STM.
Retrieval of material from semantic long term memory is an implicit process which requires clear knowledge of the time of acquisition of the semantic knowledge

correct_answer.text: Primacy effect is related to initial items receiving most consolidation

correct_answers.text: Primacy effect is related to initial items receiving most consolidation

questions.explanation:
In serial learning, the primacy effect is a tendency for the items near the beginning of the series to be better recalled than those near the middle. An accurate recollection of an item is more likely if it is one of the first (primacy effect) or last items (recency effect) to be learnt. Primacy is because initial items receive most consolidation and recency is because immediate information is still in STM. The Proactive inhibition of 'interference theory' refers to prior learning interfering with subsequent learning. Retroactive inhibition is based on the fact that over time, new memories interfere with existing ones and this interference effect is increased if there is a considerable similarity between the new memory and existing ones. The other hypothesis for forgetting is decay theory due to the trace of the memory fading with time.
Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a type of non-declarative memory?
questions.explanation:
Non-declarative memory is memory for non-declarative knowledge, involving memory systems that do not draw on the individual’s general knowledge. Non-declarative knowledge does not involve awareness and understanding of factual information about the world. It includes procedural knowledge (information about how to carry out sequences of operations – knowing how in contrast to knowing that).
Memory for factual knowledge and autobiographical events is collectively termed declarative memory. Declarative (also known as explicit) memory is of two types: episodic memory or memory for specific events (such as going to the shop this morning) and semantic memory or memory for abstract facts such as the capitals of countries.
Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015. pp. 510, 603.
Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1025.
Casey P, Kelly B. Fish’s clinical pathology: Signs and symptoms in psychiatry, 4th Edition. 2019. p. 64.

questions.question_text: A family has got a new dog. A 3 year old child in the family is afraid of dogs and would stay in the same room with the dog only if he could sit on his mother's lap and had his favourite ice cream. Select the learning theory principle employed here
questions.explanation:
The modification of a behavioural pattern by the conditioning of responses that are incompatible with the response to be eliminated is called as reciprocal inhibition. The behavioral principle of reciprocal inhibition (Wolpe) states that anxiety and relaxation cannot coexist.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 908.

questions.question_text: Identify the term that best denotes the feeling of familiarity that accompanies the return of stored material to consciousness;
questions.explanation:
Recognition is the act of process of perceiving or identifying information as matching or being the same as information that has been remembered. It is often contrasted with ‘recall’ which involves reproduction of remembered information without cues. Recognition is generally easier than recall.
Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: Which of the following can reduce groupthink?
questions.explanation:
Groupthink is a collective pattern of defensive avoidance, characteristic of group decision making in organisations in which group members develop rationalisations supporting shared illusions of their own infallibility and invulnerability with the organisation. Characteristic features include: an illusion of invulnerability, collective efforts to rationalise in order to discount warnings, an unquestioned belief in the group’s inherent morality, stereotyped views of rivals and enemies, direct pressure on any member who dissents from the consensus view, self- censorship of disagreements with the apparent group consensus, a shared illusion of unanimity, and the emergence of self-appointed protectors of the group from adverse information that might undermine the existing complacency.
Various strategies that can reduce groupthink include appointing a 'devil's advocate', encouraging open debate, acknowledging the presence of groupthink, seeking external opinion, splitting the group into smaller units for discussion, holding last chance meetings to encourage challenges, and reserving leaders' opinions until after the group's discussion has been completed.
Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: People prefer relationships that appear to offer an optimum cost benefit ratio and with expectations that our actions towards others will be reciprocated in some way. Which of the following theories suggest this?
questions.explanation:
Social exchange theory is a theory of social interaction based on the proposition that people expect rewards and costs from a social exchange to be equitable. Most of our social behaviour is influenced by the expectations that our actions towards others will be reciprocated in some way and relationships are based on a mutual exchange of benefits. The US sociologist George Caspar Homans developed this theory.
Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: The ethics to determine goodness from acts and intentions behind them rather than their consequences is
questions.explanation:
According to Immanuel Kant, a German philosopher, deontology is an ethical approach centered on rules and professional duties. Unlike many ethical theories, deontology does not focus on the consequences of individual actions. Personal emotions behind actions also do not matter with Kantian deontology because Kant believed humans do not always have rational control over their feelings. Instead, the intent behind chosen actions holds far more importance. Therefore, deontology proponents judge actions based on what people consider to be morally correct, regardless of actual consequences.
Consequentialist moral theories are teleological: they aim at some goal state and evaluate the morality of actions in terms of progress toward that state. The best-known version of consequentialism is utilitarianism. As most clearly stated by Mill a proponent of the utilitarianism (teleology), the basic principle of utilitarianism is: Actions are right to the degree that they tend to promote the greatest good for the greatest number.

questions.question_text: A patient is next on waiting list to receive CBT. A new referral comes up which needs more urgent treatment. The psychotherapist refuses to displace the next patient on the list as this would be against his sense of duty and responsibility. Which ethical principle is he upholding?
questions.explanation:
Deontic reasoning is reasoning about obligation and duty, most often in relation to ethical or moral actions, but also in forms of non-ethical problem solving. Deontology and Teleology are two alternative higher-order ethical principles concerning medical practice. The term Deontology derives from the Greek 'Deon' for 'duty' indicating the centrality of rules in governing medical practice. Accordingly, rights and duties determine action and so it is also called as absolutism. The term Teleology derives its name from the Greek 'Teleon', meaning 'purpose' and the central concept is that rather than rights, people have interests, whether these are concerns, desires or needs. Accordingly, a broad judgment of benefits and harm determine medical practice.
Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: Which of the following offers a guideline for principles of ethical research?
questions.explanation:
The World Medical Association (WMA) has developed the Declaration of Helsinki as a statement of ethical principles for medical research involving human subjects, including research on identifiable human material and data. Adopted by the WMA’s General Assembly in 1964, it is the most important set of guidelines about research on human participants. It both reflects and shapes the ethos of international research ethics. It is a living instrument and is reviewed and revised regularly. Its latest revision was in 2013.
Ref: https://www.wma.net/policies-post/wma-declaration-of-helsinki-ethical-principles-for-medical-research-involving-human-subjects/
Malik AY, Foster C. The revised Declaration of Helsinki: cosmetic or real change?. Journal of the Royal Society of Medicine. 2016 May;109(5):184-9.

questions.question_text: A 40 year old man has chest pain and dizziness. His bloods and ECG are normal. He is advised to take medications, fat restricted diet, exercise. This is called
questions.explanation:
Illness behaviour can be defined as any behaviour undertaken by an individual to relieve an experience of illness or to better define the meaning of the illness experience. Illness behaviours are considered to be the observable actions or reactions to perceived physical, emotional, or mental illness. These can include self-care or the use of healthcare services and may also include the interpretation and appraisal of symptoms, decisions to seek or delay health care, ongoing social and psychological coping strategies, adherence/concordance to recommended treatments and therapies, and the general ongoing uptake of available support services.
Ref: Murray J, Williams B. The Role of Images on Illness Behaviour: Interdisciplinary Theory, Evidence, and Ideas. Psychological Reports. 2020 Aug 5:1-23.

questions.question_text: Which of the following produced a written account on ethical aspects of medicine claiming that physicians have an obligation to protect both bodies and souls?
questions.explanation:
The oldest surviving Islamic work of medical ethics is the work of Ishaq bin Ali al-Ruhawi by the title of ‘Adab al-Tabib’ (‘Practical Doctor’s Ethics’, 9th century) which included some of the ideas of Hippocrates and Galen. This work encouraged doctors to stay away from bad influences of people, to realise that good character is much more important than wealth, and to understand that wisdom is found in moral and perfect people.
In al-Ruhawi's opinion, doctors were responsible for the protection of both bodies and souls and one of the most important obligations of doctors is to be concerned about nurturing their own body and soul. He placed great emphasis on the interaction of the mental health and physical illness, though the mind is dealt mostly in spiritual sense. Interestingly, such an idea was not entirely novel at that time in the Islamic world. Another physician Abu Baker Al-Razi gave an earlier account of the physician's moral responsibilities in his volume Akhlaq Al- Tabib, “Medical Ethics,” and the “Book of Spiritual Medicine,” bringing spiritual aspects as important part of any medical care.
Ref: Zunic L et al. Medical ethics in the medieval Islamic sciences. Journal of research in pharmacy practice. 2014 Jul;3(3):75.
Muaygil RA. Demystifying bioethics: The past, present, and future of a flourishing discipline. Journal of Nature and Science of Medicine. 2020 Oct 1;3(4):334.

questions.question_text: Which of the following model of reducing stigma demands equal rights and criminal responsibility for the mentally ill?
questions.explanation: The libertarian approach advocates equal rights with no discrimination - both positive and negative. It has the risk of inducing serial losses for the mentally ill at workplaces or courts.

questions.question_text: Tearooom Trade Study is an example of ethically controversial research practices. Which of the following was the subject of investigation in this study?
questions.explanation:
Laud Humphrey’s Tea Room Trade: Impersonal Sex in Public Places is commonly presented in many sociological methods texts as an example of covert and deceptive research methods that endangered subjects without their consent. However, from the vantage point of beneficence as well as from a concern with social justice, Humphrey’s tearoom study made significant positive contributions to the population he studied. His thorough fieldwork exploded the myth that the populations of men engaging in these casual sexual encounters were criminals, transients, or predatory paedophiles that communities needed to hunt down and criminally prosecute. Humphrey’s work seriously questioned the received view that homosexual contact should be subjected to the retributive harms of imprisonment and ultimately created doubt in the dichotomous categories of gender that closely paralleled sexual behaviour.
Ref: Lenza M. Controversies surrounding Laud Humphreys’ tearoom trade: An unsettling example of politics and power in methodological critiques. International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy. 2004.

questions.question_text: The nurses in your ward do not like a newly admitted patient. They are angry that she is trying to split them up by giving conflicting messages at ward rounds. Which of the following phenomenon is likely?
questions.explanation: Morgan (1979) coined the term malignant alienation to describe a process characterised by a progressive deterioration in the relationship between carers (staff in a ward) and a patient, including loss of sympathy and support from members of staff, who tended to construe these patients' behaviour as provocative, unreasonable, or overdependent. In some instances, such alienation may precede suicide/ attempted suicide of the patient (Excerpt from Watts & Morgan, Br J Psychiatry. 1994 Jan;164(1):11-5. http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8137091)

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is a feature of atypical Anorexia Nervosa?
questions.explanation:
In atypical anorexia nervosa (DSM-5), all the criteria for anorexia nervosa are met, except that despite significant weight loss, the individual’s weight is within or above the normal range.
Ref: American Psychiatric Association. Diagnostic and statistical manual of mental disorders (DSM-5®). American Psychiatric Pub; 2013 May 22.

questions.question_text: Bleuler discarded the term dementia praecox primarily because

options.text: Mania was commonly coexistent with dementia praecox
Not all cases began during adolescence
Praecox affect was rarely seen in the early cases
No treatment was available for dementia praecox
No cognitive impairment was noted in the early cases

correct_answer.text: Not all cases began during adolescence

correct_answers.text: Not all cases began during adolescence

questions.explanation:
In 1911, a book was published by Eugen Bleuler describing in detail asylum patients under his care who met clinical criteria for the psychotic disorder named Dementia Praecox by Emil Kraepelin. Bleuler followed Kraepelin and became the major figure to describe the characteristics of this syndrome in young adults, taking issue with Kraepelin on two points. He felt that cases of dementia praecox did not always arise in adolescence (praecox), nor did they always progress to intellectual dullness (dementia).
Ref: McGlashan TH. Eugen Bleuler: centennial anniversary of his 1911 publication of Dementia Praecox or the group of schizophrenias. Schizophrenia bulletin. 2011 Nov 1;37(6):1101-3.

questions.question_text: Mrs. Z arrives at work at least an hour earlier than anyone else to plan the day. She becomes visibly upset if the cleaners have moved anything on her desk and in her office, which is very tidy. This has led to some of her colleagues completely avoiding her office space. Her home and car are spotlessly clean. This is best described as
questions.explanation: Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder (OCPD) is a personality disorder characterized by excessive perfectionism and a need for control over one's environment. People with OCPD tend to be reliable and orderly, but also inflexible and unable to surrender control. This makes it hard for people with this condition to express their feelings, have close relationships and enjoy their successes. This lady is exhibiting some of the above traits.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true with respect to adjustment disorder?

options.text: correlates with the severity of the stressor
occurs more often in males than in females
it is a type of bereavement

questions.explanation: Although an adjustment disorder can occur at any age, it is more common at times in life when major transitions occur, such as adolescence, mid-life, and late-life (Mental Health: Adjustment Disorder - WebMD, http://www.webmd.com/mental-health/mental-health- adjustment-disorder).

questions.question_text: With respect to models of diagnostic classification, which of the following is correct?

options.text: Ontological theories suggest that mental state does not exist by virtue of its abstract nature
Fulford claims that psychiatric diagnoses are not value laden
Pheneticists stress on the natural existence of hierarchical structure among disease entities
Categorical entities are not used in modern classification

correct_answer.text: Ontological theories suggest that mental state does not exist by virtue of its abstract nature

correct_answers.text: Ontological theories suggest that mental state does not exist by virtue of its abstract nature

questions.explanation: In contrast to the essentialist strategy that treats diseases as entities that exist in nature and form natural groups in essence, phenetic approach, (also called numerical taxonomy) shifts the emphasis to the systematic description of the observed disease presentations to enable manual classification. This approach treats all characters and attributes as having equal weight. While ICD and DSM are atheoretical in terms of assuming aetiology and causal models, they are not entirely atheoretical in descriptions used (e.g. dissociative disorder, conversion, etc. employ psychodynamic concepts).

questions.question_text: Which of the following assessment is not a part of MMSE?
questions.explanation:
The MMSE is a 30-point cognitive test developed in the mid-1970s to provide a bedside assessment of a broad array of cognitive functions, including orientation, attention, memory, construction, and language. It does not include clock drawing.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 45.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a frontal lobe test?
questions.explanation:
Cognitive estimate testing assesses frontal lobe functioning. The patient is asked a question that requires abstract reasoning and cannot be answered by general knowledge alone (e.g. ‘how many camels are there in the UK?’).
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 88.

questions.question_text: Subtracting 7 out of 100 repeatedly (serial sevens test) is most useful to test one's
questions.explanation:
Concentration can be tested by starting at 100 and counting backward by 7 (or 3). It can also be tested by saying the letters of the alphabet backward starting with Z or by naming the months of the year backward starting with December.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 11.

questions.question_text: A 56-year-old woman is brought to the hospital with a stroke. A CT scan shows evidence of left occipital lobe damage. Which of the following is most likely to be seen?
questions.explanation: ‘Cortical blindness’ was first used by Gordon Holmes in 1918 to describe visual impairment of soldiers who were blind secondary to injuries to the occipital cortex. Cortical blindness is the total or partial loss of vision in a normal-appearing eye caused by damage to the occipital cortex of the brain. Cortical blindness can be acquired or congenital, and may also be transient in certain instances. Acquired cortical blindness is most often caused by loss of blood flow to the occipital cortex from either unilateral or bilateral posterior cerebral artery blockage due to ischemic stroke. In most cases, the patient may recover some of their vision.

questions.question_text: A boxer is knocked out by a blow to his lateral skull. Despite recovering after a few minutes, and being asymptomatic for the next 12 hours, he develops severe headache, vomiting and reduced consciousness. Which of the following is the most indicated investigation?
questions.explanation:
The CT image is determined by the degree to which tissues absorb X-irradiation. This technique is particularly good at distinguishing between bones, blood vessels, and organs, so can well detect bone traumas, tumours, and haemorrhage. In a CT scan, CSF appears black, brain tissue appears grey, and the skull appears white. Blood appears bright white. As CT is quicker and relatively cheaper than MRI, it is far more commonly used in acute settings where medical stability still needs to be ascertained. In cases of suspected bony fracture and fresh hemorrhage, a CT scan is more useful than plain X-ray which cannot pick up the bleed, or MRI brain which is slower to obtain and may miss fresh bleeding.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 69.
Martinelli C, Shergill SS. Everything you wanted to know about neuroimaging and psychiatry, but were afraid to ask. BJPsych Advances. 2015 Jul;21(4):251-60.

questions.question_text: Hyperhomocysteinemia is associated with increased risk for which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Elevated plasma total homocysteine is a modifiable risk factor for development of cognitive decline, dementia, and Alzheimer’s disease in older persons. In a variety of clinical studies, the relative risk of dementia in elderly people for moderately raised homocysteine ranges from 1.1.5 to 2.5, and the Population Attributable risk ranges from 4.3 to 31%. Intervention trials in elderly with cognitive impairment show that homocysteine-lowering treatment with B vitamins markedly slows the rate of whole and regional brain atrophy and also slows cognitive decline. The findings are consistent with moderately raised plasma total homocysteine, which is common in the elderly, being one of the causes of age-related cognitive decline and dementia. Thus, the public health significance of raised tHcy in the elderly should not be underestimated, since it is easy, inexpensive, and safe to treat with B vitamins.
Ref: Smith AD et al. Homocysteine and dementia: an international consensus statement. Journal of Alzheimer's Disease. 2018 Jan 1;62(2):561-70.

questions.question_text: Which of following is not commonly seen in nicotinic acid deficiency?
questions.explanation:
Pellagra is a condition caused by low levels of niacin (nicotinic acid) or its precursor tryptophan. Niacin deficiency results in the condition of pellagra, which includes the triad or ‘three D’s’: dermatitis, dementia, diarrhoea (related to mucosal atrophy), and can result in death. Similar to a sunburn, brown discolouration and lesions on the skin typically exposed to the sun such as hands, elbows, knees, and feet are present ('Casal's Necklace'). Initially, neurological changes such as anxiety, poor concentration, fatigue, and depression can manifest (due to reduced serotonin synthesis), but as pellagra advances, dementia and delirium may occur. Also, gastrointestinal complications, glossitis, cheilosis, stomatitis, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhoea (or less commonly constipation) may be present.
Ref: DeRight J. Vitamin Deficiencies. In Essential Neuropsychology: A Concise Handbook for Adult Practitioners 2022 (pp. 317-321). Springer, Cham.

questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes ideomotor apraxia?

options.text: Inability to coordinate and carry out facial and lip movements
Inability to construct elements to a meaningful whole
Inability to perform a multiple-step task

questions.explanation:
Ideomotor apraxia is characterised by the impaired ability to imitate unfamiliar actions. It is also called motor apraxia or ideokinetic apraxia. Ideomotor apraxia results from damage to the dominant parietal lobe. Abnormalities include (i) abnormal amplitude of motor movements (ii) body-part-as-object substitution, e.g. the patient uses his own finger to represent a toothbrush when asked to brush his teeth; (iii) abnormal orientation of body parts when attempting to perform an action.
Ref: Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4th Edition. 2015.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true regarding screening for alcohol problems?

options.text: Most patients give inaccurate drinking histories
There are high rates of detection of alcohol problems in primary care and hospital settings
Rates of detection are improved by asking routine alcohol-screening questions
Diseases related to alcohol abuse respond poorly to early detection and intervention
At-risk groups should not be specifically targeted for screening

correct_answer.text: Rates of detection are improved by asking routine alcohol-screening questions

correct_answers.text: Rates of detection are improved by asking routine alcohol-screening questions

questions.explanation:
Diseases related to alcohol abuse are common, significant, and amenable to improvement by early detection and intervention. There are low rates of detection in primary care and hospital settings, which may be improved by increased vigilance, increased awareness of alcohol problems, awareness of routes of referral, asking routine alcohol screening questions, and paying special attention to at-risk groups. Many patients give reasonably accurate drinking histories if asked, although some may underestimate consumption.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 582.

questions.question_text: A patient with schizoaffective disorder is on both lithium and risperidone. He develops tremors as a side effect of his treatment. Which of the following will help detecting the offending agent?
questions.explanation: EPSE with risperidone can cause tremors (Parkinsonian) and rigidity, unlike Lithium tremor where one would not expect rigidity.

questions.question_text: When asked where do he lived when he was a child, a patient replied "Winchester. Manchester City was my favourite football team." The type of speech abnormality exhibited is
questions.explanation:
This is an example of clang association. Clang association is an abnormality of speech where the connection between words is their sound, rather than their meaning. This may occur during manic flight of ideas.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 104.

questions.question_text: Capgras syndrome (l'illusion des soies) is:

options.text: Also called the phantom mirror image

questions.explanation:
Capgras syndrome (l’illusion des sosies) is a type of delusional misidentification in which the patient believes that a person known to them has been replaced by a ‘double’ who is to all external appearances identical but is not the ‘real person’.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 105.

questions.question_text: A 20-year-old man is unable to express his problem coherently but appears very confused and feels that 'something is happening but not sure what it is'. This sense of perplexity and uncertainty that exists during a prodrome of psychosis may be linked most appropriately to which of the following experiences?
questions.explanation:
Delusional mood is recalled as arising following a period when there is an abnormal mood state characterised by anticipatory anxiety, a sense of ‘something is about to happen’ and an increased sense of the significance of minor events. The development of the formed delusion may come as a relief to the patient in this situation.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 107.

questions.question_text: A 23-year-old man notices the inscribed image of the Queen on a coin, and says "I know now, my mother is an alien". This is an example of
questions.explanation:
A delusional perception is a primary delusion which is recalled as having arisen as a result of a perception (e.g. a patient who, on seeing two white cars pull up in front of his house, became convinced that he was therefore about to be wrongly accused of being a paedophile). The percept is a real external object, not a hallucinatory experience.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 107.

questions.question_text: A 43-year-old woman, who was involved in a serious flight accident, felt at the time of the accident as if she had become unreal. For some time, she felt as if something had changed and that she was not herself. This is known as:
questions.explanation:
Depersonalisation is an unpleasant subjective experience where the patient feels as if they have become ‘unreal’. It is a feeling that one is not oneself or that something has changed. Often this is associated with a feeling of unreality, so that the environment is experienced as flat, dull, and unreal (known as ‘derealisation’). Many people who complain of depersonalisation also state that their capacity for feeling is diminished or absent. This is a subjective experience because to the outside observer there is no loss of ability to respond emotionally and appropriately to any given situation. Depersonalisation is not a delusion, and it should be distinguished from nihilistic delusions in which the patient denies that they exist or that they are alive, or that the work or other people exist. Depersonalisation is a non-specific symptom occurring in many psychiatric disorders, as well as in ‘normal’ people.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 108.
Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 10.
Casey P, Kelly B. Fish’s clinical pathology: Signs and symptoms in psychiatry, 4th Edition. 2019. pp. 81-82.

Depersonalisation is frequently accompanied by the symptom of derealisation
Depersonalisation can be an experience of normal healthy people
