questions.question_text: Of various thought disorders classified by Andreasen, which of the following are more common in schizophrenia than mania?
questions.explanation:
Nancy Andreasen created a scale in which the classic formal thought disorders are subdivided into three groups:
Communication disturbances: when the speaker does not meet the necessary requirements for the listener’s understanding (poverty of content of speech, pressure of speech, distractible speech, tangentiality, derailment, stilted speech, echolalia, self-reference, circumstantiality, loss of goal, perseveration, and blocking)
Language disturbances: when the speaker violates the semantic and syntactic conventions (incoherence, clang association, neologisms, use of word approximations)
Thought disturbances: when only thinking alone seems affected (poverty of thought and illogically aberrant inferential processes)
Andreasen demonstrated that these psychopathological findings were not specific to schizophrenia and were also common in other mental disorders (e.g. mania). Of those listed, derailment (synonymous with loose associations - a symptom of schizophrenic thought disorder in which there is a total break in the chain of association between the meaning of thoughts) is more common in schizophrenia than mania.
Ref: Jerónimo J et al. Formal Thought Disorders–Historical Roots. Frontiers in psychiatry. 2018 Nov 9;9:572.
Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 108.
Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 10.

questions.question_text: The phenomenon in which a subject perceives other people's heads to be as big as their actual body size can be termed as
questions.explanation:
Dysmegalopsia refers to a change in the perceived shape of an object. Some authors reserve the terms ‘dysmegalopsia’ to describe objects that are perceived to be larger (or smaller) on one side than the other, while others use the term generically to describe any change in perceived size.
Ref: Casey P, Kelly B. Fish’s clinical pathology: Signs and symptoms in psychiatry, 4th Edition. 2019. p. 25.

questions.question_text: A patient repeats whatever the examiner says. He is exhibiting
questions.explanation:
Echolalia is the repetition of phrases or sentences spoken by others (e.g., the examiner). It is an echophenomenon that may be seen in catatonia. Other echophenomena are echopraxia (repeating what you do) and mirror movements (doing as you do at the same time).
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 109.

questions.question_text: The nature of speech produced in Broca aphasia is

options.text: Effortful but with grammatical use of language

questions.explanation:
Broca aphasia (also called non-fluent or expressive aphasia) had traditionally been characterised by non-fluent speech and impaired repetition but intact auditory comprehension. It has long been thought to be associated with damage to Broca area (i.e. left inferior frontal convolution) or Brodmann area 44. Broca aphasia is characterised by retained use of nouns and verbs, but the patient may have lost all forms of pronouns, articles, and conjunctions, and hence may struggle to speak more than one word at a time even with enormous effort.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 48.

questions.question_text: Mr X was admitted to the psychiatric unit with a history of elated mood, overactivity, restlessness, grandiose delusions, disinhibited behaviour and was diagnosed with mania. A student nurse observed that he also experienced third person auditory hallucinations and wondered whether first rank symptoms could occur in manic patients. He wanted to clarify this with the treating psychiatric doctor in the team. Choose the most appropriate statement from the following:

options.text: First rank symptoms never occur in manic patients
First rank symptoms may present in 10-25% of manic patients
First rank symptoms are very rarely seen in manic patients
First rank symptoms are present in all cases of mania with psychosis
First rank symptoms are present in nearly half of all patients with mania

correct_answer.text: First rank symptoms may present in 10-25% of manic patients

correct_answers.text: First rank symptoms may present in 10-25% of manic patients

questions.explanation:
First rank symptoms are a group of symptoms that have special significance in the diagnosis of schizophrenia. They are useful because they occur reasonably often in schizophrenia and more rarely in other disorders, and it is not too difficult to tell whether they are present or not. However, there is no symptom that is pathognomonic of schizophrenia. First rank symptoms can all be reported in other conditions (e.g. organic psychoses, manic illnesses). First rank symptoms are present in approximately 10-30% of patients with mania.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 110.
Channa A et al. First rank symptoms in Mania: An indistinct diagnostic strand. Acta Medica International. 2016 Jul 1;3(2):20.

questions.question_text: Compulsory treatment cannot be justified under which of the following ethical principles?
questions.explanation:
A fundamental principle of medical care is that treatment of a patient should be with their consent. A patient has a right to decide for themselves which treatments to undergo and which treatments to refuse (autonomy). This right is retained, even when the refusal of treatment could result in death or significant deterioration in health. Treatment without consent is possible only in certain circumstances, constrained by appropriate laws.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 936.
